title: Pergamum (Revelation 2:12–17)
hook: a white stone with a new name only you know

segments.voice: Yesterday, Smyrna: a church poor on paper, rich in the letter's eyes, told to be faithful unto death. Your line was a crown of life. What small thing did you stay faithful in? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

A small white stone. That's the gift at the end of today's letter, and the letter never says what it means. The next letter in Revelation goes to the church in Pergamum, a city the King James Bible spells Pergamos. The risen Christ speaks as the one with the sharp sword with two edges. And the first thing he says isn't a complaint. He says he knows their address: "where Satan's seat is." A hard place to live. Then, at the very end, comes a strange promise: a white stone, and on it a new name that only the one who receives it knows. Today's word is the city that letter was sent to.

Start with where they lived. The letter says they "holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith." It names one man, Antipas, "my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." That's all the text tells us about him. What Satan's seat was, it doesn't say. Some readers point to the city's great altars and temples; others to the worship of the emperor. The letter leaves it there. Second, the trouble. Not everyone in this church held the same line. The letter warns about some who held the teaching of Balaam, the hired prophet from the book of Numbers, and others who held the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Faithful under pressure from outside, and still muddled inside. Both are true of the same church, and the letter says both. Third, the promise, in the King James words: "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it." Hidden manna reaches back to the bread in the wilderness. The white stone, readers have guessed at. Some think of a white pebble a juror cast to acquit. Some think of a token that let a guest into a feast. The text doesn't explain. Fourth, the name. In the Bible, people are renamed at turning points: Abram becomes Abraham, Jacob becomes Israel, and Jesus calls Simon Peter. Here the new name isn't announced to the crowd. It's written on a stone and known only to the one who holds it. Other people may know someone by a job, a reputation, a worst day. This letter says there's a name none of them gets to read.
screen: `A NEW NAME ONLY ONE PERSON KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick up a small stone. If there's one nearby, from a path, a plant pot, a pocket, hold it in your palm. If not, close your hand around anything small and plain. Settle, and breathe. Feel its weight, its edges, how it warms in your hand. Then let a question rest there, without answering it in words: what would be written on it by someone who knew you all the way through? Not your title. Not your mistakes. If you pray, you can hold the stone and simply listen. If you don't, just hold it, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Pergamum. A church holding fast in a hard place, warned about its muddle, and promised hidden manna and a white stone with a new name on it.

Your line: a new name. Today, keep a small stone in your pocket, and each time your hand finds it, remember the name on the stone that nobody else gets to read. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the seven letters of Revelation 2–3 both as messages to real early churches and as words for churches today, and Bible study groups sometimes take them one letter at a time.

original.note: Greek: a small stone, a pebble. the white stone of Revelation 2:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: a white stone is a strange, random detail.
what it means: a gift for those who overcome, with a new name on it that only the receiver knows.
what a scholar hears: psephos, a pebble. readers have suggested a juror's white stone for acquittal or a token of entry to a feast; the text itself doesn't say.

notes: The index uses 'Pergamum'; the KJV spells it 'Pergamos' (said in the hook). Confirm.

Readings of 'Satan's seat' (altars and temples; emperor worship) and of the white stone (juror's acquittal pebble; token of entry to a feast) are given as 'some readers' guesses, unranked. Confirm they are fairly described.
Balaam is called 'the hired prophet from the book of Numbers' (Numbers 22–24; cf. Revelation 2:14). Confirm the description is acceptable.
Original: ψῆφος glossed as 'a small stone, a pebble'. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Editor pass: cut the superlative 'stranger than any before it' and 'nobody can say/be sure' claims in favor of what the text says; replaced the stock 'isn't the last word' carry ending with a concrete image.

Audit pass: the hook no longer says the city was promised the stone (2:17 promises it 'to him that overcometh'); the renaming line no longer credits God with Simon's new name (John 1:42 gives it to Jesus); trimmed a doubled 'the text doesn't explain'.
